The marketer airs an infomercial for the device with repeated references to the fact that the product is “FDA Approved,” alongside claims that “in just 10 minutes a day for 30 days, you can effortlessly lose two or more inches and 10 pounds from your waist.” The infomercial is deceptive because the juxtaposition of the “FDA Approved” reference and claims about weight loss and reduction in waist circumference gives the impression that the FDA has found the product to be effective for such dramatic effects. 
 5. Third-Party Literature 
 The FTC doesn’t regulate the content or accuracy of statements made in independently written and published books, articles, or other non-commercial literature. The FTC does, however, prohibit the deceptive use of such materials in the marketing of products. Marketers of dietary supplements and other health products should be aware that the use of newspaper articles, abstracts of scientific studies, or other third-party literature to promote a particular brand or product can have an impact on how consumers interpret an ad and on what claims the marketer will be responsible for substantiating. [59] The determination of whether information provided through such materials will be subject to FTC jurisdiction turns largely on whether the materials have been created or are being used by a marketer specifically for the purpose of promoting its product. [60] While each case will be fact-specific, marketers may be legally responsible for claims implied by their reference either directly or indirectly to third-party literature. 
 Example 50: An author publishes a book on the curative properties of an herb. The book’s title is “The Miracle Cancer Cure.” The book doesn’t endorse or otherwise mention any particular supplement brand. The author/publisher doesn’t sell the herbal supplement and doesn’t have a material connection to any marketers of the herb. As non-commercial speech, the book itself wouldn’t be subject to the FTC’s jurisdiction over advertising. However, if a marketer of the herb quotes the title of the book and uses excerpts to describe the anti-cancer benefits of its product, such references would be considered advertising. The marketer would be responsible for substantiating any claims about its product that are conveyed by these references. 
 Example 51: The marketer of the herb described in Example 50 provides a link to a web page that in turn links to the “Miracle Cancer Cure” book. The fact that the book is “two clicks” away from the marketer’s own website doesn’t insulate the marketer from responsibility for substantiating any implied claims that consumers may take from the indirect reference to the book. The FTC will evaluate the marketer’s website, the description it provides in linking indirectly to the book, statements appearing on the linked page, and other elements of the marketing to determine whether the marketer is using references to the book to promote its product. 
 Example 52: Advertising for a weight-loss supplement includes references to what appears to be an independent website discussing the risks of gastric bypass surgery and referencing the advertiser’s supplement as a safer alternative. In fact, the advertiser created and owns the gastric bypass website and does not disclose that financial relationship. The website is not independent third-party literature. The advertiser is responsible for the accuracy of claims made on the site and must clearly and conspicuously disclose its ownership of the site. 
 For purposes of dietary supplement labeling, Section 5 of DSHEA provides an exemption from labeling requirements for scientific journal articles, books, and other publications used in the sale of dietary supplements, provided these materials are reprinted in their entirety, aren’t false or misleading, don’t promote a specific brand or manufacturer, are presented with other materials to create a balanced view of the scientific information, and are physically separate from the supplements being sold. While the DSHEA third-party literature provision doesn’t provide an exemption from FTC requirements for other forms of advertising, as a practical matter, publications and other materials that comply with the elements of the provision, particularly with the requirement that such materials be truthful, not misleading, and balanced, are also likely to comply with FTC advertising law. 
 IV. Conclusion 
 Marketers of health-related products, including dietary supplements, should be familiar with the requirements under both FDA law and FTC law that labeling and advertising claims be truthful, not misleading, and substantiated. The FTC approach generally requires that health-related claims be backed by competent and reliable scientific evidence substantiating that the representations are true. To ensure compliance with FTC law, marketers of any health-related product should follow two important steps: 1) Consider what express and implied messages consumers are likely to take from your ads. Where appropriate, carefully qualify your claims – in other words, clearly explain the limited circumstances in which the advertised benefits or results apply; 2) Carefully review the support for each claim to make sure it is scientifically sound, adequate in the context of the surrounding body of evidence, and relevant to the specific product and advertising claim.

class="help-content"> <a name="ad-policy-claims"></a> <h1>Claims and substantiation</h1> <div> <p class="lead">Learn how to ensure that advertising claims are accurate and provide substantiation when required.</p> <p>This policy covers general claims, including books and healthcare.</p> <dfn class="anchor-policyreqs"></dfn> <h2 class="otp">Policy requirements</h2> <p>Advertisers are required to ensure the accuracy of claims and provide factual substantiation if requested by Amazon.</p> <dfn class="anchor-prohibitcontent"></dfn> <h2 class="otp">Prohibited content</h2> <p>We prohibit the following claims in all ads:</p> <ul class="a-vertical"> <li> <span class="a-list-item">Ads for weight management are prohibited from suggesting that the product alone (such as without diet, exercise, or a calorie-controlled diet) can be used to achieve results or that a weight loss product is effective for everyone.</span> </li> <li> <span class="a-list-item">Ads for weight management are prohibited from guaranteeing permanent weight loss, a specific rate of weight loss, or promising that weight wonât be regained after stopping the product.</span> </li> <li> <span class="a-list-item">Ads must avoid content that encourages unhealthy eating habits or negative body image and are prohibited from using before and after imagery.</span> </li> <li> <span class="a-list-item">Claims that non-prescription products are as effective as prescription products.</span> </li> <li> <span class="a-list-item">Regulatory endorsement claims on healthcare products.</span> </li> <li> <span class="a-list-item">Any book that includes claims to cure a high-risk disease or ailment.</span> </li> </ul> <p></p> <dfn class="anchor-restrictcontent"></dfn> <h2 class="otp">Restricted content</h2> <p>We permit environmental claims, origin claims, warranties or guarantees, and claims that describe health or quality ingredients on ingestible products such as gluten free or organic. These claims must be substantiated on the ad creative, product detail page, or landing page, and environmental claims must be dated within 24 months.</p> <p>We also require substantiation for the following types of claims on healthcare products (excluding personal care products) across all Amazon ad products and all on supply. This requirement also applies to over-the-counter (OTC) products when making certain claims:</p> <ul class="a-vertical"> <li> <span class="a-list-item"><strong>Product effectiveness:</strong> claims that describe the effectiveness of a product (for example, "<em>Decreases cholesterol levels by 25%</em>") and are typically based on objective evidence or scientific data. If the claim is on the product packaging, no further substantiation is needed. Otherwise, substantiation, including source and date (no age requirement), is required in the ad creative, on product packaging or landing page.</span> </li> <li> <span class="a-list-item"><strong>Product endorsements</strong>: Medical or professional society endorsements (for example, "<em>#1 physician recommended allergy medicine</em>"). If the claim is on the product packaging, no further substantiation is needed. Otherwise, substantiation, including source and date (within 24 months), is required in the ad creative, on product packaging, or landing page.</span> </li> <li> <span class="a-list-item"><strong>Comparative claims</strong>: Claims that compare a product or service to a competitorâs product (for example, "<em>Provides 50% more pain relief than the leading brand</em>"). If the claim is on the product packaging, no further substantiation is needed. Otherwise, substantiation, including source and date (within 24 months), is required in the ad creative, on product packaging, or landing page.</span> </li> </ul> <p></p> <dfn class="anchor-countryrestrict"></dfn> <h2 class="otp">Country-specific restrictions</h2> <div class="wrapper"> <dfn class="header-adssectionExpander-1">Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, and Sweden</dfn> <div class="adssectionExpander-1"> <p>Energy-Efficiency Labels are required on large electric appliances. Advertisers are responsible for ensuring energy-efficiency labels are present in their ads and compliant with the laws in their locale; Amazon will reactively remove any noncompliant ads reactively. Amazon will ensure that ASIN-based ads have compliant labels; products may be blocked from some ads placements until auto-labeling is developed for that placement. Please review <a href="https://europa.eu/youreurope/business/product-requirements/labels-markings/energy-labels/index_en.htm" target="_blank">EU Guidance here</a>.</p> </div> <dfn class="header-adssectionExpander-2">Brazil</dfn> <div class="adssectionExpander-2"> <p>Any products described as âorganicâ must include the logo on the product packaging. Any consumable described as âdietâ âsugar freeâ âlow sugarâ âlightâ or similar must include the same claim on the product packaging.</p> </div> <dfn class="header-adssectionExpander-3">Singapore</dfn> <div class="adssectionExpander-3"> <p>Any product described as âorganicâ must include a âcertified organic' logo on the product packaging.</p> </div> <dfn class="header-adssectionExpander-4">United Kingdom</dfn> <div class="adssectionExpander-4"> <p> </p> <ul class="a-vertical"> <li> <span class="a-list-item">Energy-Efficiency Labels are required on large electric appliances.
